title: Ketones and Hypoglycemia: βHB, C-Peptide and the Whole-Blood Trap
summary: Apply the 2024 DKA criteria and measure β-hydroxybutyrate rather than nitroprusside strips, work up hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia with C-peptide, proinsulin and a sulfonylurea screen, and convert whole-blood to plasma glucose.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 17 Hits 3–7 and 9 and Traps 2–4. Checked against Umpierrez 2024 (consensus, Diabetologia copy), Sacks 2011 (NACB/ADA laboratory guidelines), Jensen 2012 (ENETS), Peltola 2018 and Leighton 2017. Hit 3 and Trap 3 equate high insulin + high C-peptide with insulinoma; ENETS and Peltola 2018 require excluding sulfonylureas (register flag rv-cpeptide-sulfonylurea). Hit 6 uses glucose ≤ 55 mg/dL from a guideline not read here; the lesson teaches ENETS (≤ 40 mg/dL). Hit 7 says whole blood is 10–15% lower; Sacks 2011 gives ~11%. Not taught: glycated albumin being better standardized, 1,5-anhydroglucitol, and the 10:1 βHB:AcAc figure.

objectives: Apply the 2024 adult DKA criteria and explain why β-hydroxybutyrate should be measured directly.
Interpret insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin in hypoglycemia, including the sulfonylurea exception.
State the ENETS biochemical criteria for insulinoma during a supervised fast.
Convert between whole-blood and plasma glucose and choose fructosamine when HbA1c is unreliable.

scenes.title: A negative strip and a high insulin
scenes.altText: Two patient cards. Patient A: type 1 diabetes, vomiting, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, glucose 410 mg/dL; urine ketone strip only “trace.” Patient B: a nurse with recurrent fainting; glucose 38 mg/dL, insulin very high. Question tokens: “Is A’s DKA ruled out?” and “Is B an insulinoma?” The cartoon scientist holds a ketone strip in one hand and a C-peptide tube in the other.

cues.text: Patient A has type 1 diabetes and is vomiting. pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12, glucose 410. Yet the urine ketone strip reads only trace.
Patient B, a nurse, keeps fainting. Glucose 38 milligrams per decilitre, and insulin is very high.
Does a weak strip rule out DKA? Does high insulin mean a tumour? Both answers depend on what the test actually measures.

scenes.title: Three ketones, and C-peptide’s receipt
scenes.altText: A ketone panel (schematic): acetoacetate (AcAc), β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB) and acetone. Normally AcAc and βHB are roughly equimolar; a high-NADH state (DKA, fasting, hypoxia, alcoholic ketoacidosis) shifts the balance toward βHB. A strip card: nitroprusside reacts with AcAc (and with acetone if glycine is added) — it cannot detect βHB. A C-peptide card: proinsulin is cleaved into insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts; injected insulin carries no C-peptide. A glucose card: plasma glucose is about 11% higher than whole-blood glucose at a normal hematocrit.

cues.text: The body makes three ketone bodies: acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a little acetone. Normally acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are roughly equal.
In DKA, fasting, hypoxia or alcoholic ketoacidosis, high NADH shifts the balance toward beta-hydroxybutyrate.
The common nitroprusside strip reacts with acetoacetate, and with acetone if glycine is added. It cannot detect beta-hydroxybutyrate at all.
C-peptide is insulin’s receipt. Proinsulin is cut into insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts, but insulin from a syringe brings no C-peptide.
And one conversion: plasma glucose runs about 11 percent higher than whole-blood glucose when the hematocrit is normal.

scenes.title: DKA: measure the ketone that matters
scenes.altText: A DKA criteria card (2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus): D — glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL or known diabetes; K — β-hydroxybutyrate ≥ 3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥ 2+; A — pH < 7.3 and/or bicarbonate < 18 mmol/L. Notes: βHB ≥ 3.0 mmol/L has > 90% sensitivity and specificity; the consensus recommends direct βHB for diagnosis and monitoring. As DKA resolves, βHB converts to AcAc, so a strip can look worse while the patient improves. Captopril and valproate can give false-positive nitroprusside tests. About 10% of DKA is euglycaemic (< 200 mg/dL), e.g., with SGLT2 inhibitors. Patient A: βHB 6.4 mmol/L → DKA.

cues.text: The 2024 consensus defines DKA with three letters. D: glucose of 200 or more, or known diabetes. K: beta-hydroxybutyrate of 3.0 millimoles per litre or more, or urine ketones 2 plus. A: pH below 7.3 and or bicarbonate below 18.
Beta-hydroxybutyrate of 3.0 or more is over 90 percent sensitive and specific, and the consensus recommends measuring it directly for diagnosis and monitoring.
As DKA resolves, beta-hydroxybutyrate is converted to acetoacetate, so a strip can look worse while the patient is getting better.
Strips also mislead the other way: captopril and valproate can give false positives. And about one DKA in ten is euglycaemic, with glucose under 200, for example on SGLT2 inhibitors.
Patient A’s beta-hydroxybutyrate is 6.4. With her pH and bicarbonate, that is DKA, whatever the strip said.

scenes.title: Hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia: insulin, C-peptide, drugs
scenes.altText: A decision tree, drawn at the time of hypoglycemia. Whipple’s triad: symptoms, low glucose, relief with glucose. High insulin + LOW C-peptide → exogenous insulin. High insulin + HIGH C-peptide → endogenous: insulinoma OR sulfonylurea/meglitinide — screen for the drug. ENETS 2012 criteria for insulinoma during a supervised fast (72-hour fast = classical gold standard): glucose ≤ 40 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L); insulin ≥ 6 µU/mL (≥ 3 by ICMA); C-peptide ≥ 200 pmol/L (≈ 0.6 ng/mL); proinsulin ≥ 5 pmol/L; βHB ≤ 2.7 mmol/L; no sulfonylurea in plasma or urine. Back to the hook: B’s C-peptide is undetectable → injected insulin. A fructosamine card: glycated serum proteins reflect 15–30 days, useful when HbA1c is unreliable.

cues.text: For hypoglycemia, draw the samples during the episode. Whipple’s triad: symptoms, a low glucose, and relief when glucose is given.
High insulin with low C-peptide means injected insulin. High insulin with high C-peptide means the pancreas is secreting it: an insulinoma, or a sulfonylurea. Screen for the drug.
In a supervised fast, the classical 72-hour fast, the ENETS criteria are glucose 40 or less, insulin 6 or more, C-peptide 200 picomoles per litre or more, and proinsulin 5 or more.
Plus beta-hydroxybutyrate 2.7 or less, and no sulfonylurea in blood or urine. Patient B’s C-peptide is undetectable: injected insulin.
One more glycemia marker: fructosamine, glycated serum protein, reflects the last 15 to 30 days and helps when HbA1c cannot be trusted.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Urine ketone strip negative → no DKA” (✓ strips miss βHB; measure βHB directly); “High insulin + high C-peptide = insulinoma” (✓ also sulfonylureas — run a drug screen); “POC whole-blood glucose 110 = plasma glucose 110” (✓ plasma ≈ 11% higher; ≈ 122 mg/dL).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative urine ketone strip rules out DKA. Strips cannot see beta-hydroxybutyrate. Measure it directly.
Trap two: high insulin with high C-peptide proves insulinoma. Sulfonylureas give the same pattern. Run a drug screen.
Trap three: a whole-blood glucose of 110 is the same as plasma glucose 110. Plasma runs about 11 percent higher, roughly 122.

scenes.title: The strip is blind to Beta; C-peptide is the receipt
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The strip is blind to Beta. C-peptide is the receipt — no receipt, the insulin came from outside.” A strip token with a blindfold over βHB, a receipt token. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the strip is blind to beta. And C-peptide is the receipt: no receipt means the insulin came from outside.

Where it breaks: a receipt does not prove a tumour, because sulfonylureas also produce one; proinsulin and beta-hydroxybutyrate criteria add specificity; and urine ketones of 2 plus still count in the DKA criteria.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “DKA: glucose ≥ 200 or DM · βHB ≥ 3.0 · pH < 7.3 and/or HCO₃ < 18 — measure βHB, not strips”, “Insulin ↑ C-pep ↓ = injected · both ↑ = insulinoma or sulfonylurea · plasma glucose ≈ 11% > whole blood”.

cues.text: Measure beta-hydroxybutyrate, not nitroprusside strips, in DKA; read insulin with C-peptide and a sulfonylurea screen; and remember plasma glucose runs about 11 percent above whole blood.

props.label: DKA: glucose ≥ 200/DM · βHB ≥ 3.0 · pH < 7.3 and/or HCO₃ < 18 — measure βHB
Insulin ↑ C-pep ↓ = injected · both ↑ = insulinoma or sulfonylurea · plasma ≈ +11%

explanation.what: Plain language: DKA is diagnosed by high sugar, high ketones and acid blood; the common urine strip misses the main ketone. Low sugar with high insulin can be injected insulin, a tumour or a pill, and C-peptide helps tell them apart. Scientific terms: acetoacetate (AcAc), β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB), nitroprusside reaction, C-peptide, proinsulin, Whipple’s triad, supervised 72-hour fast, fructosamine.
explanation.why: High hepatic NADH in DKA shifts AcAc to βHB, which nitroprusside cannot detect; during recovery βHB is reconverted to AcAc. Proinsulin is cleaved into insulin and C-peptide in equimolar amounts, so endogenous secretion (insulinoma or sulfonylurea-stimulated) raises both, while injected insulin raises insulin alone. Plasma contains about 11% more water than whole blood.
explanation.measure: DKA (2024): glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL or known diabetes; βHB ≥ 3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥ 2+; pH < 7.3 and/or HCO₃ < 18 mmol/L. ENETS insulinoma: glucose ≤ 40 mg/dL, insulin ≥ 6 µU/mL (≥ 3 µU/mL ICMA), C-peptide ≥ 200 pmol/L, proinsulin ≥ 5 pmol/L, βHB ≤ 2.7 mmol/L, negative sulfonylurea screen. Plasma glucose ≈ 1.11 × whole-blood glucose at normal hematocrit. Fructosamine reflects 15–30 days.
explanation.differs: Exogenous insulin (insulin ↑, C-peptide ↓) vs insulinoma or sulfonylurea (insulin ↑, C-peptide ↑; drug screen separates). DKA vs euglycaemic DKA (glucose < 200, e.g., SGLT2 inhibitors).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: nitroprusside vs βHB, DKA criteria, insulin/C-peptide patterns, Whipple’s triad and the 72-hour fast, and whole-blood vs plasma glucose.

mnemonic.explanation: Nitroprusside strips cannot detect β-hydroxybutyrate; C-peptide accompanies only the body’s own insulin.

questions.stem: A patient with DKA has improved clinically and her pH is rising, but the urine ketone strip has gone from 1+ to 3+. What best explains this?

options.text: β-Hydroxybutyrate is being converted to acetoacetate, which the strip detects
options.rationale: Correct. As DKA resolves, βHB is oxidized to AcAc, so nitroprusside reactions can rise while the patient improves.
Incorrect. The rising strip reflects a shift between ketones, not more ketones; follow βHB directly.
Incorrect. This is an expected effect of the method.

questions.stem: During hypoglycemia (glucose 35 mg/dL), insulin is 48 µU/mL, C-peptide is 1,100 pmol/L and proinsulin is raised. What is the most important next laboratory test?

options.text: A sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen in plasma or urine
options.rationale: Correct. Endogenous hyperinsulinism (high C-peptide) fits insulinoma or a sulfonylurea; the drug screen separates them.

options.text: No further testing; this proves insulinoma
options.rationale: Incorrect. Sulfonylureas produce the same pattern.

options.text: Insulin antibodies to prove injected insulin
options.rationale: Incorrect. A high C-peptide argues against injected insulin.
Incorrect. HbA1c does not explain an acute hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A point-of-care meter calibrated to whole blood reads 110 mg/dL in a patient with a normal hematocrit. Approximately what plasma glucose does this correspond to?

options.rationale: Correct. Plasma glucose is ~11% higher than whole-blood glucose at a normal hematocrit (110 × 1.11 ≈ 122).
Incorrect. Whole blood and plasma differ by about 11%.
Incorrect. Plasma is higher, not lower, than whole blood.
Incorrect. The difference is about 11%, not 50%.

references.usedFor: DKA criteria (D glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L [200 mg/dL] or history of diabetes; K βHB ≥ 3.0 mmol/L or ketonuria ≥ 2+; A pH < 7.3 and/or HCO₃ < 18 mmol/L); nitroprusside measures AcAc not βHB; strips can mislead during recovery; captopril and valproate false positives; direct βHB recommended; βHB ≥ 3.0 > 90% sensitivity and specificity; ~10% euglycaemic DKA, SGLT2 inhibitors.

references.citation: Sacks DB, Arnold M, Bakris GL, et al. Guidelines and recommendations for laboratory analysis in the diagnosis and management of diabetes mellitus. Diabetes Care. 2011;34(6):e61-e99.
references.usedFor: Plasma water ~11% higher than whole blood → plasma glucose ~11% higher at normal hematocrit; βHB and AcAc normally equimolar, shifted toward βHB in DKA, fasting, hypoxia, alcoholic ketoacidosis; nitroprusside measures AcAc (acetone with glycine), cannot measure βHB; fructosamine/glycated albumin reflect 15–30 days.

references.citation: Jensen RT, Cadiot G, Brandi ML, et al. ENETS consensus guidelines for the management of patients with digestive neuroendocrine neoplasms: functional pancreatic endocrine tumor syndromes. Neuroendocrinology. 2012;95(2):98-119.
references.usedFor: Whipple’s triad; six criteria (glucose ≤ 2.2 mmol/L [≤ 40 mg/dL], insulin ≥ 6 µU/mL [≥ 3 by ICMA], C-peptide ≥ 200 pmol/L, proinsulin ≥ 5 pmol/L, βHB ≤ 2.7 mmol/L, no sulfonylurea); 72-hour fast classical gold standard.

references.citation: Peltola E, Hannula P, Huhtala H, et al. Characteristics and outcomes of 79 patients with an insulinoma: a nationwide retrospective study in Finland. Int J Endocrinol. 2018;2018:2059481.
references.usedFor: Whipple’s triad; low glucose with inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide; βHB ≤ 2.7 and negative oral hypoglycemic agent screen distinguish endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia; 72-hour fast gold standard.

references.citation: Leighton E, Sainsbury CA, Jones GC. A practical review of C-peptide testing in diabetes. Diabetes Ther. 2017;8(3):475-487.
references.usedFor: C-peptide cleaved from proinsulin and co-secreted in equimolar amounts with endogenous insulin; not a product of administered insulin; cornerstone in insulinoma and factitious hypoglycemia assessment.

claims.text: 2024 DKA criteria; nitroprusside detects AcAc not βHB; recovery shift; captopril/valproate false positives; βHB ≥ 3.0 > 90% sens/spec; ~10% euglycaemic DKA.
AcAc and βHB normally equimolar; high NADH (DKA, fasting, hypoxia, alcoholic ketoacidosis) shifts toward βHB.
C-peptide equimolar with endogenous insulin, absent from injected insulin; high insulin + high C-peptide = endogenous (insulinoma or sulfonylurea).
Plasma glucose ≈ 11% higher than whole blood; fructosamine reflects 15–30 days.
Glucose ≤ 55 mg/dL threshold; glycated albumin better standardized; 1,5-anhydroglucitol 1–2 weeks; whole blood 10–15% lower.
